title: The terms we get from psychology

entries.note: Freud's school, a young discipline of little more than a century whose coiners gave us many common words; Jung's related school is [[see:analytic psychology]].
Latin-sounding term introduced by Freud's English translators for his plain German [[from:Es]], meaning simply 'the it'.
English translators' Latinised rendering of Freud's German [[from:Ich]], simply 'the I'.
Translators' Latinised version of Freud's [[from:Über-Ich]], literally the super I or above I.
Freud's actual German term, plain German for 'the it', which English translators turned into [[gave:id]].
Freud's German word, simply 'the I', rendered in English as [[gave:ego]].
Freud's German term meaning the super I or above I, translated into English as [[gave:super ego]].
One of Freud's main translators, who rendered his German terms in Latinised forms like [[see:id]] and [[see:ego]].
Another primary translator of Freud who turned his German words into more Latinised terms such as [[see:id]].

From German Narzissmus, after [[from:Narcissus]]; first used clinically by [[see:Paul Näcke]] for sexual self-attraction, earlier used by [[see:Samuel Taylor Coleridge]] for vanity; now therapy-speak weapon.
Coined in German by [[from:Eugen Bleuler]] as opposite of [[see:equivalence]], strength on both sides; now 'skunked', meaning both conflicted and not caring.
Patients redirecting feelings from earlier relationships onto the analyst; the English rendering of Freud's German [[from:Übertragung]].
Freud's German word for [[gave:transference]], literally a carrying over or 'over-dragging'; also used for transferring money.
Freud's German word, later rendered with Latin elements as [[gave:repression]].
Psychological term associated with Freud, built from Latin elements after he used German [[from:Verdrängung]]; now common in armchair psychology.
Freud's interest, meaning things you don't know you're thinking; often confused with [[see:subconscious]], with which it has merged.
Often wrongly attributed to Freud, who actually wrote of the [[see:unconscious]]; the two concepts have since merged.
Freud's idea that boys unconsciously want to kill their father and sleep with their mother, named after [[from:Oedipus]]; the inverse is the [[see:Electra complex]].
Greek mythical king who unknowingly killed his father [[see:Laius]] and married his mother [[see:Jocasta]]; pronunciation differs across the Atlantic.
Jung's counterpart to the [[see:Oedipus complex]], a girl's rivalry with her mother for her father, named after [[from:Electra]]; widely discredited.
The name of Jung's school of thought, as distinct from Freud's [[see:psychoanalysis]].
One of Freud's developmental stages, which tied the psyche to bodily functions such as eating.
One of Freud's developmental stages; fixation at it underlies the idiom [[gave:anally retentive]].
One of Freud's stages, when children form the early attachments and rivalries Jung linked to the [[see:Electra complex]].
One of the developmental stages in Freud's bodily theory of the psyche.
The last of Freud's developmental stages named in the episode.
An everyday expression that unknowingly refers to Freud's theory of fixation at the [[from:anal stage]].
Saying someone has a complex uses Jungian vocabulary.
Jung turned it from an adjective into a noun; from intro, inward, contrasting with [[see:extrovert]].
Made a noun by Jung, who disliked this spelling as bad Latin and preferred extravert, from extra, outward; contrasts with [[see:introvert]].
The play telling [[see:Oedipus]]'s story, also called Oedipus Tyrannus, King Oedipus, the title he eventually earns.
Oedipus's father, ruler of Thebes, who tried to have baby [[see:Oedipus]] killed and was later slain by him on the road.
Wife of Laius and mother of [[see:Oedipus]], whom he unknowingly married; she killed herself when the truth came out.
King of Corinth who adopted the abandoned [[see:Oedipus]].
Set [[see:Oedipus]] an unsolved riddle about an animal with two, three or four feet; his answer, man, won him the throne of Thebes.
Daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra who helped kill her mother to avenge her father; the source of the [[see:Electra complex]].
Sitcom both hosts love; Niles jokes that as a Jungian, unlike Freudian Frasier, there'll be no blaming mother, illustrating the [[see:Oedipus complex]].
Handsome youth of Greek myth cursed to love his own reflection in a pool, loved in vain by [[see:Echo]]; source of [[gave:narcissism]].
Credited by Freud with first using [[see:narcissism]] clinically, for a sexual perversion of attraction to one's own body.
Poet who is the earliest citation for both [[see:narcissism]] and [[see:narcissine]], before clinical use.
A form alongside [[same-root:narcissism]] first found in Coleridge's poetry, meaning behaving like Narcissus.
Echo speech, repeating others' words, normal in learning to talk but also an adult symptom; named after the nymph [[from:Echo]].
Chatty nymph cursed by Hera to repeat others' words; pining for [[see:Narcissus]], she faded to a voice, hence the echo and [[gave:echolalia]].
A baby's version of banana: borrowed words stressed on the second syllable confuse learners, an example tied to [[see:echolalia]]; compare [[see:puter]].
Baby form of computer, dropping the unexpected unstressed first syllable, like [[see:nana]].
Coined by [[see:Georges Gilles de la Tourette]] for involuntary obscene language in neurological patients; literally dung speech, sharing -lalia with [[same-root:echolalia]].
Late 19th-century coiner of [[see:coprolalia]], whose surname gave [[see:Tourette's syndrome]].
Named after [[from:Georges Gilles de la Tourette]]; poorly understood when [[see:coprolalia]] was coined, it's now known not to require obscenity.
Shares the dung element of [[same-root:coprolalia]] but means attraction to it.
Ancient Greek for soul and the name of the soul's goddess, a mortal princess loved by [[see:Eros]] and set tasks by [[see:Aphrodite]].
Falls in love with [[see:psyche]] and finally makes her immortal after finding her in the underworld.
Sets Psyche tasks such as sorting grains, done by ants, and collecting golden fleece, in the myth of [[see:psyche]].
Like [[see:psyche]], means breath, life and spirit; De Anima's principle organising living bodies fed into late 19th-century psychology terms.
A literary term that Jung applied to family figures like the mother and father.
Now the study of the mind but literally the study of the soul, from [[from:psyche]]; a recent coinage unknown to the ancient Greeks.
England's 1845 act, reflecting older unkind terms based on the idea that the moon caused moods; compare [[see:lunatic]].
Rooted in the idea of moods inspired by the moon; once clinical, later insulting, and the source of [[gave:loony]].
Moon-caused madness; the idea goes back to Old English [[see:moon sick]], but the word itself comes from Paradise Lost.
Old English word for lunacy, literally moon sick, showing the moon-madness idea is ancient; compare [[see:moon sickness]].
Another Old English term for moon-induced madness, alongside [[see:moon sick]].
A variation on [[from:lunatic]], an example of clinical words becoming insults.
Used by [[see:Thomas Sutton]] for alcohol's psychological effects; from Latin [[from:delirare]], to go off the furrow, i.e. off the rails.
British physician who tried to clinicalise mental health, using [[see:delirious]] for the symptoms of alcohol abuse.
Famous Belgian brewery with a pink elephant logo, recalled through [[see:delirium tremens]].
The shakes from alcohol abuse, the state where you see pink elephants; previously discussed on the show.
Swiss psychiatrist, full name Paul Eugen Bleuler, who coined [[see:schizophrenia]], [[see:ambivalence]] and [[see:autism]] in German.
Coined in German by [[see:Eugen Bleuler]], who also spoke of plural schizophrenias, replacing [[see:dementia praecox]]; meaning a splitting of the mind.
Earlier name for the condition Bleuler renamed [[see:schizophrenia]].
Bleuler created [[see:ambivalence]] as a spin-off and opposite of this word.
Coined by [[see:Eugen Bleuler]] for detachment from reality in schizophrenia; applied in 1938 by [[see:Hans Asperger]] to the condition now so called.
Applied [[see:autism]] in 1938 to the modern condition; his name gave the former term [[see:Asperger's syndrome]].
Former term from [[from:Hans Asperger]], used for a while in child psychology for a condition similar to [[see:autism]], no longer used.
The fear of long words, dismissed as a made-up phobia with silly multilingual roots.
From Greek [[from:phobos]], fear or literally flight; phobias first appeared in Greek medical contexts and should be somewhat irrational.
One of the earliest English phobia words, from the 14th century, meaning rabies, whose sufferers can't physically swallow.
Like [[see:homophobia]], more a bias than a fear, but rooted in the notion of fear, from psychology terminology entering public discourse.
Originally fear of humans, from Latin homo, used of animals; reinterpreted via Greek homos, same, as fear and then hatred of gay people.
Shows the Latin homo, human, which the original sense of [[see:homophobia]] used, related to [[same-root:hominid]].
Related to Latin homo, human, as in the original sense of [[see:homophobia]].
Uses the unrelated Greek homos, same, like most English homo- words, which shifted the meaning of [[see:homophobia]].
Another word with Greek homos, same, unlike the Latin homo of [[see:Homo sapiens]].
Could be misread as attraction to men, but means attraction to the same, from Greek homos, explaining [[see:homophobia]]'s shift.
Also known as kinks; the DSM-5 lists them as well as phobias.
Online said to mean fear of peanut butter sticking to the roof of the mouth, but literally just fear of peanut butter.
Literally fear of ducks, said to mean fear a duck is secretly watching you, from a [[see:The Far Side]] comic; compare [[same-root:anatiferous]].
Comic thought to have given [[see:anatidaephobia]] its sense of fearing a duck is watching you.
Producing ducks, in Samuel Johnson's dictionary and discussed in their dictionary episode; possibly linked to the belief in [[see:barnacle geese]] born from trees.
Their supposed birth from trees and barnacles was speculated as the reason for [[see:anatiferous]].
Also hamaxophobia, fear of riding in a car, from a Greek root meaning carriage.
Fear of failure, from a Greek root meaning unfortunate.
Fear of ugliness, from Greek [[from:kakos]], bad; related to [[same-root:cacophony]] and [[same-root:caca]], from a PIE root meaning defecate.
Jess first linked it to [[see:cacophobia]], then corrected herself: kakos comes from a PIE root meaning defecate, not the same root.
Bad sound, from the same Greek kakos as [[same-root:cacophobia]].
Contrast to [[see:cacophobia]]; online said to be fear of hearing good news, but literally just good phobia.
Related to the root of [[same-root:cacophobia]].
Fear of being ridiculed, which everyone has a little of; a phobia only if intense and irrational.
Fear of work, with the ergo of [[same-root:ergonomics]]; one who has it is an ergophobe.
Discussed on a previous occasion when the hosts talked about ergo.
Named after the [[from:agora]], ancient Greece's massive meeting place, so fear of large places full of people; mentioned in an earlier episode.
Pop-culturalised fear of very big things, celebrated on subreddits, like the stomach-drop at a wide shot of a blue whale.
A silly coinage meaning fear of phobias.
Fear of Friday the 13th, from Greek paraskevi, Friday, and dekatria, thirteen.
Fear of the great mole rat; the hosts don't know why it exists.
Imprecise, superficial everyday use of clinical psychotherapy language, often by privileged people online, sometimes weaponised, as in [[see:set boundaries]].
A [[see:therapy speak]] phrase misused to disguise coercive control, as in [[see:Jonah Hill]]'s leaked texts listing his 'boundaries' for his girlfriend.
An example of [[see:therapy speak]] used outside therapy sessions.
Cited as an example of [[see:therapy speak]] in everyday use.
One of the dangers people are warned about in [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed with gaslighting and narcissism as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
A [[see:therapy speak]] label now often used to describe people you disagree with.
Listed as a label people misuse in [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Being 'a bit depressed' is cited as casual [[see:therapy speak]] that drains clinical precision.
Calling a liking for cleanliness 'a bit OCD' is [[see:therapy speak]] that may frustrate people with the severe disorder.
Being 'a bit bipolar' is cited as casual [[see:therapy speak]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Actor whose 2023 leaked texts to surfer Sarah Brady used [[see:set boundaries]] language to disguise coercive control.
Coined to encourage social awareness but taken up by others as an insult, a parallel to weaponised [[see:therapy speak]].
An early clinical term for mental disability, once not an insult, that pejorated into one, like [[see:loony]].
From a therapist's 2023 TikTok on breaking up with a friend, criticised as clinicians teaching weaponised [[see:therapy speak]].
